source.title: Prediction Risk and Estimation Risk of the Ridgeless Least Squares Estimator under General Assumptions on Regression Errors

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and symbols are garbled in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes ridgeless linear regression rather than deep networks and reports risk behavior across model sizes and in the overparameterized regime, bearing on the general double-descent version.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports test MSE across model specifications and noise conditions. Its accompanying training-error curves help locate the interpolation threshold but are not separate test-risk results. Figures 2 and 3 report variance-component comparisons across error covariance structures; these do not sweep model size, epochs, or sample size. Figure 4 and the accompanying theory discuss overparameterized risk behavior.
record.test_reason: The study gives a real-data result in a non-deep model class: ridgeless least squares on ACS 2018 group wages. Figure 1 shows test MSE across 7 specifications (p = 209 to 2,182) crossing p = n = 1,415, and the authors describe it as double descent. This is a new setting with a result bearing on V4, so T3 rather than T2. The main contribution is about the variance under non-i.i.d. errors, which fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors read Figure 1 as suggesting that double descent is universal across degrees of clustered dependence, provided the total error variance is unchanged. Remark 4.1 and Figure 4 show only the overparameterized side analytically: variance Θ(1/(γ−1)) blows up as γ→1 and vanishes as γ grows, while bias stays bounded.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimum-norm linear regression theoretically and uses ACS group-level regression specifications; it does not reproduce a deep-network experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: In the ACS experiment, test-error curves are reported as nearly identical across the tested clustered-noise levels, especially for p > n.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a left-spherical design, the expected variance of ridgeless prediction and estimation risk depends on the error covariance only through Tr(Ω), matching simulations for AR(1) and clustered errors. In Figure 1, the test-error curves are nearly unchanged across clustering levels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For ridgeless least squares, double-descent risk curves depend on the regression-error covariance only through its trace, not through serial or clustered dependence.

record.problems: The ACS size sweep has seven specifications, and the plotted values are not stated numerically. The theoretical results assume a left-spherical design; the authors identify this as a limitation.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 training-error curves were not extracted as rows because they are not test-risk outcomes. Figure 4's plotted variance and bias components were not recorded as separate total-risk rows.

untested.parts: n is fixed; no sample-size sweep.
Only linear ridgeless regression is tested, not multiple model classes. The total-risk curve on either side of p = n is not reported numerically.
No effective-complexity measure predicting the peak across axes.
Not tested: the effect of noise amplitude on the total-risk peak, multiple peaks, and optimal regularization. Figure 4 only shows variance components scaling with Tr(Ω)/n in the p > n regime.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 4, Corollary 4.4 and Remark 4.1 are declared in rows_left_out. They give an analytic and simulated descent for p > n: variance diverges at the interpolation point and scales with Tr(Ω)/n = 1, 2, 4. This weakly bears on V4 (second descent) and on the variance-driven part of V6, but reports components, not total risk. If these are later extracted as rows, V6 could gain a link. Text extraction garbles equations.

versions.untested_parts: Increasing training-sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests linear-regression settings, not a range of model classes; it does not establish that the pattern holds across model classes generally.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting the peak across size, epochs, and sample size.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimal regularization removes the peak.
Whether recounting complexity using an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
